Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

panelspatialprobit 0.0.0.9000

  • First implementation (plan phases 0-3):
    • Model fitting:
      • psprobit() and psoprobit() for balanced panels.
      • SAR, SDM, SLX and non-spatial specifications.
      • Pooled or random effects, Mundlak correlated random effects and time effects.
    • Methods and helpers:
      • psp_impacts(), with the spatialreg::impacts() method, for direct, indirect and total effects on probabilities.
      • Methods: summary(), predict(), coef(), vcov(), confint(), plot(), tidy(), glance() and as_draws().
      • sim_psprobit(), psp_weights() and rook_weights().
    • Engine: a sampler with residual-update latent sweeps, a collapsed griddy Gibbs step for rho, a half-Cauchy random-effects prior, a transformation move for the cut-points and a generalised-Gibbs scale move.
  • Completion of phases 2-3:
    • Chamberlain correlated random effects: cre = list(type = "chamberlain", vars = ~ x1).
    • psp_impacts() gains type = "unit" (impacts conditional on the random effects, using random-effect draws kept by the sampler) and by_period = TRUE (impacts within each period).
    • psp_classification(): in-sample hit rate, AUC, Brier score and confusion table; reported by summary().
    • summary() of ordered models also shows the thresholds in the MASS::polr parameterisation.
    • psp_control(progress = ) prints sampling progress.
    • Vignettes “Getting started with panel spatial probit” and “Ordered outcomes”.
  • Spatial error models (phase 4): model = "sem", "sdem" and "sarar", with optional error weights M and a lambda prior (psp_priors(lambda =), psp_control(lambda_range =)). The engine now works with the general operator A = (I - lambda M)(I - rho W), and impacts and predictions account for the error term in the latent variance.
  • Dynamic models (phase 5): dynamic = psp_dynamic() adds the lagged outcome (and optionally its spatial lag), with Wooldridge (2005) initial conditions by default. sim_psprobit() gains gamma and eta for lagged outcomes and lambda / M for spatial errors.
  • Missing outcomes are imputed through their latent values (phase 6).
  • predict(newdata = ) gives counterfactual predictions for the fitted units and periods (phase 6).
  • psp_ppc(): posterior predictive checks of category shares, Moran’s I and persistence per period (phase 6).
  • The griddy Gibbs step for rho and lambda locates the posterior on a coarse pass before refining, about 5x faster for small panels.
  • Time-varying spatial weights (phase 6): W (and M) may be a list with one matrix per period. Durbin terms, the spatial lag of the lagged outcome, impacts, predictions and posterior predictive checks use the weights of each period.
  • Spatially autocorrelated random effects (phase 4): effects = "spatial_random" gives alpha = phi W alpha + a, with a phi prior in psp_priors(phi = ). sim_psprobit() gains phi.
  • psp_response_path() (phase 5): how a temporary or permanent change in a regressor propagates over time in a dynamic model, by simulating the outcome histories under the baseline and the shock with common random numbers.
  • Experimental approximate likelihood (phase 6): psp_loglik(), logLik() (and so AIC() / BIC()) and psp_dic(). The likelihood is estimated with the GHK simulator on the sparse precision of the latent outcomes, with the random effects integrated out.
  • Student-t latent errors (phase 4): errors = psp_t(df) (robit for binary outcomes), sampled as a scale mixture of normals with fixed degrees of freedom. Probabilities and impacts average over simulated mixing variances (psp_control(mixture_draws = )); fit$v_mean flags outlying observations. sim_psprobit() gains df.
  • Latent AR(1) dynamics (phase 5): psp_dynamic(latent = TRUE) gives z_t = rho W z_t + gamma z_{t-1} + X_t beta + alpha + u_t (coefficient lag_z), with probabilities, impacts, predictions, response paths and the approximate likelihood integrating over the latent history. sim_psprobit() gains gamma_z.
  • New vignettes (phase 7): “Interpreting impacts”, “Dynamic panel spatial probit” and “How we validated the samplers” (reference sampler, SBC, Monte Carlo study, a replication of the Wang and Kockelman (2009) simulation, and cross-checks; drawn from summaries written by validation/vignette_data.R).
  • summary() prints effective sample sizes as whole numbers.
  • The engine is written in Rust (it was C++ with RcppEigen). Installing from source needs Cargo and rustc >= 1.84 (https://rustup.rs). Changes:
    • Chains run in parallel threads on every operating system, Windows included (psp_control(cores = )); the draws do not depend on cores.
    • New psp_control(threads_per_chain = ): the sweep over the latent variables updates the periods of a chain in parallel, each period with its own random number substream, so the draws do not depend on it either. With 4 threads, a binary SAR fit with N = 10,000 and T = 20 runs 3 times as fast as with the C++ engine.
    • The sampler is faster on one core: per iteration, 1.3 to 1.5 times faster than the C++ engine at N = 1,000 and 1.4 to 2 times at N = 10,000 (SEM models gain most, from a supernodal Cholesky factor of the random-effects precision).
    • psp_impacts(), predict(), psp_ppc(), psp_response_path() and psp_loglik() run in Rust (1.3 to 18 times faster on one core) and in parallel over the workers of future::plan() (see ?psp_control); their results do not depend on the plan.
    • The sampler always uses inversion normals, whatever RNGkind(normal.kind = ) says.
    • For the same seed, fits, psp_ppc(), psp_response_path() and psp_loglik() give different (still reproducible) numbers: the latent sweep draws from one substream per period, and the post-processing from package streams rather than R’s generator.
